title: Thoughts from Alert Bay
article: My name is Diane Bell. I am a lifetime resident of Alert Bay. I am a member of the 'Namgis First Nation, through my grandmother, Winnie Bell (nee Cook).

My grandfather, Robbie Bell, was the youngest son of Chief Jim Bell, of Village Island. My gran Bell was the daughter of half- breed parents, Steven Cook (part English, part Namgis, part Mowachalt), and her mom, Jane Cook, the eldest daughter of Chief Whonnock of the Kwakiutl tribe, who lived in Cluxewe.
Jane was a renowned translator who travelled to Victoria with the McKenna McBride Commission as the only woman delegate. She championed the rights of Firsts Nations people, in particular, the women.
In addition Steven and Jane were both pillars of the Anglican Church. My gran, Emma Hunt, was married to Chief Thomas Hunt of Fort Rupert.
Her mother was Koskimo/'Namgis, Misa (Edith Nelson), and her father was Dr. Billy, a shaman of the Friendly Cove, or Mowachalt people.
My grampa descended from a long line of chiefs, with a link to his Tlingit great grandmother of Tongass, Alaska.
My dear uncle, George Hunt, is now the hereditary chief of our family. Misa married my step-grampa, Pop (Gideon) Whonnock, who also came from the Kwakiutl.
This then is the context out of which I speak. I live in Alert Bay, but my roots are in most of the villages of the Kwakwala- speaking people.
Generally, as First Nations people, we have many concerns. High unemployment, poverty, poor housing, alarming health problems.
In my own case, my father, Chris Bell, was a tragic victim, dying under mysterious circumstances while in the care of Victoria police.
In my mind's eye, I can still recall vividly the autopsy photos of his bruised body, where he was found in a cell made icy by a broken window, with broken glass particles found in his hair.
Who knows what despair led my dad to lead a life of homelessness and alcoholism on the streets of Victoria.

My cousin, Joe Peters, also died tragically in the hands of RCMP. Lorraine Jacobson, a young mother and daughter of our Whe-La-La-U Nation, also died at the end of a gun. Another cousin, Anthany Dawson, died in custody.
The stories are endless, of First Nations people dying before their time, often in dealings with police.
What has been the outcome of all of this? Inquests, inquests and more inquests. The recommendations are usually, cause of death, inconclusive.
No fault to anyone. More cross-cultural training and sensitivity for police, RCMP.
We attend these inquests, with hopes and dreams, that now, in the new millennium, 2005, that our voices will be heard. Some of us live in more fear, because of the power of the uniform and the gun.
I now will address the column by Tommy Sewid. He is a close relative, in that his grampa was Chief James Sewid, an honorable, and generous leader, who was the brother of my grampa Robbie.
I appreciate that Tommy is an entrepreneur, and takes groups to Village Island and traditional territory. My dear friend Emma Tamlin spoke to me about Tommy's letter to the editor (Gazette, Feb. 2).

She asked me to write a letter, to state the hurt that the Elders and many of us who are from Village Island feel about what we believe is a desecration of our traditional birthplace, not unlike the biblical story, of the merchants in the temple.

In the words of his grampa's biography, "Guests Never Leave Hungry", I implore Tommy to really think about what is happening at Village Island. This letter is an open invitation, to anyone who cares to know or visit our lands, to speak to us, and we will guide you there for free.
I would like to at this time, wonder at the punitive articles re: Pearl Hunt, school board rep from Alert Bay.
I would suggest perhaps that the school board meetings rotate, and take place in Alert Bay as well.
I commend Pearl, as she is the administrator of the Whe-la-la-U. I know she was very involved in the investigation and subsequent inquest into the death of Lorraine Jacobson.
In conclusion, I will now speak of the Orca Sand and Gravel Project and the KTFC (Kwakiutl Territorial Fisheries Commission).

I believe that the lands and waters of our area are sacred, and should be treated with care and kindness. We drink clean water, and can still catch natural salmon, dig clams, jig for cod, harvest sea urchins, hunt for deer and elk.

I have attended many meetings, and conducted my own research about the proposed gravel quarry at Cluxewe. In communications with the Bella Coola Nation, who turned down this type of project, and with other First Nations, I am deeply concerned about the long-term environmental impact this is going to have on our area.
I have asked how much will revenue be? How much will we make? How many jobs?
I have been told that is impossible to predict, as the market for gravel in the States is so volatile. I will be speaking at the hearings which are upcoming.
I know nothing about the dealings of the KTFC, as we, the 'Namgis, pulled out of the organization.
I did see our honorable Chief Bill Cranmer, satirized, in a doghouse cartoon, last year.
I would ask the Gazette to interview all parties involved, so that as a reader, I can be informed in a more balanced way.
